strengths: Substantial conceptual contribution: this paper is the first to establish second-order and path-length regret bounds for online episodic tabular MDPs, filling a notable gap relative to the broader online learning literature where such data-dependent guarantees are standard.

Comprehensive best-of-both-worlds results: a single algorithmic framework (OFTRL with log-barrier regularization and optimistic loss/Q estimators) simultaneously achieves first-order, second-order, and path-length bounds in the adversarial regime and variance-aware gap-independent and gap-dependent bounds (polylog(T)) in the stochastic regime with adversarial corruption, for both global optimization and policy optimization.

Concrete technical improvements over prior art: the gap-dependent bound removes the 1/min Δ dependence of Jin et al. (2021) via variance adaptation, the lower-order term H^3 S^2 A^2 log^2(T) of Dann et al. (2023b) is improved to H^2 S^2 A log^2(T), and the variance measures V, V^c are shown to be H^2-sharper than prior Var*(s,a)-based notions (Appendix B.2).
Matching lower bounds (Ω(√SAL⋆), Ω(√SAQ∞), Ω(√HV1), Ω(√SAVT)) certify near-optimality of the global-optimization upper bounds and meaningfully ground the new complexity measures.

Transparent presentation: clear motivation, well-organized comparison tables (Tables 1-3), careful exposition of the three key technical components (dilated bonuses, virtual episodes, optimistic Q-estimator), and extensive, detailed proofs in appendices. Limitations (known transitions, H-gap in policy optimization, path-length gap) are explicitly and honestly discussed.
Reproducibility of algorithms is adequate: both algorithms are fully specified with all constants, learning-rate updates, and loss predictions, and all assumptions are stated.
weaknesses: Restriction to known transition kernels: the main results hold only when P is known; the paper itself notes that even first-order guarantees for policy optimization under unknown transitions remain open, so the reach of the contribution in the practical/unknown-dynamics setting is limited (though honestly acknowledged).

The policy-optimization bounds retain an extra H factor relative to global optimization (e.g., √H²SA vs √SA leading terms, and an H factor in the variance-aware gap-dependent bound), consistent with the known H-gap but meaningfully weaker than the global-optimization guarantees.

The path-length upper bound leaves a √(SA/H)-dependent gap to the lower bound Ω(√HV1), and the variance-aware gap-dependent bound in Theorem 4.2 carries additional non-leading terms (√(HS²A²C log T), H^{1/2}S^{3/2}A^{3/2} log^{3/2} T); full tightness is not achieved in these aspects.

Minor presentation/cross-referencing sloppiness that could confuse readers: several lemmas are cited as 'Theorem' (e.g., Theorems C.2, C.3, C.4, D.4, E.1, F.4, F.9), and remarks are cross-referenced with theorem numbers (e.g., 'Theorem 4.3' and 'Theorem 5.4' are actually Remarks 4.3/5.4; Remark D.11 restates 'Theorem 4.3').

Purely theoretical contribution with no empirical validation; while common for this line of work, the practical benefit of the data-dependent adaptivity (e.g., whether polylog(T) behavior materializes on realistic instances) is not demonstrated.

Some lower-bound results (Section 6) follow from a fairly simple truncation reduction applied to the known minimax lower bound, so their technical depth is modest, though they are appropriate and sufficient for the stated purpose.

strengths: The paper addresses a well-motivated and clearly stated open question: whether a single best-of-both-worlds algorithm for online episodic tabular MDPs can achieve first-order, second-order, and path-length regret bounds in the adversarial regime together with variance-dependent (gap-independent and gap-dependent) bounds in the stochastic regime. The contributions (Tables 1-3) are positioned precisely against prior work (Zimin and Neu 2013; Lee et al. 2020; Jin et al. 2021; Luo et al. 2021; Dann et al. 2023b).

The paper delivers what it claims: the first second-order and path-length bounds for online episodic tabular MDPs, for both global optimization (OFTRL over occupancy measures with log-barrier regularizers and loss-shifting adapted to OFTRL) and policy optimization (a new optimistic Q-function estimator with a subtracted margin γ_t H/q_t(s) that makes the estimator provably optimistic in expectation). The technical ingredients (dilated bonuses, virtual episodes, adaptive log-barrier learning rates) are carefully combined and well explained in Section 5.1.

The gap-dependent stochastic bound improves over Jin et al. (2021) by removing the 1/min Δ dependence, and the variance measures (occupancy-weighted variance V and conditional V^c) are convincingly argued to be H^2-sharper than existing Var*(s,a)-based measures (Section B.2).

The lower bounds (Theorems 6.1 and 6.2, proved via a clean truncation reduction and a generalized instance construction in Lemma G.2) match the global-optimization upper bounds up to logarithmic factors for L*, Q∞, and V, establishing near-optimality of the main results.

The appendix (roughly 65 pages) contains complete, largely self-contained proofs, a notation table, and explicit comparisons with existing variance notions, supporting reproducibility and verifiability.
weaknesses: Restriction to known transition kernels substantially limits the scope. The paper itself acknowledges that even first-order data-dependent guarantees under unknown transitions remain open (Dann et al. 2023b), so all results apply only to the easier known-dynamics setting; the title and abstract could make this limitation more prominent.

The policy-optimization results carry an extra factor of H (and log^2(T)) relative to the global-optimization results, and closing this H-gap is left open; the path-length upper bound leaves an explicit √(SA/H)-dependent gap versus the lower bound Ω(√(H V1)). These gaps are honestly discussed but reduce the reach of the contribution.

There are internal inconsistencies between the main text and the appendix that undermine confidence in the stated constants: e.g., the restatement Theorem E.15 of Theorem 5.3 has different corruption-dependent lower-order terms than the main-text statement; Remark D.11 and Remark E.16 claim the bound 'improves by a factor of H' yet display a UVar formula still containing H; several cross-references miscall lemmas as theorems (Theorem D.4/F.1/F.2 vs. Lemma D.4/F.1/F.2); and at least one proof step appears typographically incorrect (e.g., 'p_τ(s,a) ≤ log(SAT)' on p. 25).

The variance-aware gap-dependent bounds in the corrupted regime carry sizable lower-order terms (e.g., √(H S^2 A^2 C log^{3/2}(T)) and H^{1/2} S^{3/2} A^{3/2} log^{3/2}(T)), and the improvement by a factor of H in Remarks 4.3/5.4 requires an additional assumption (uncorrelated losses across layers), which weakens the practical appeal of the refined bounds.

The contribution is of a specialized, incremental nature for the learning-theory community: the framework (OFTRL + log-barrier + loss-shifting + dilated bonuses) is assembled from known components (Jin et al. 2021; Luo et al. 2021; Dann et al. 2023b; Ito et al. 2022a), with the novelty concentrated in adapting the analysis to refined data-dependent measures. Significance is real but niche, and no experiments are included (acceptable for a theory paper but limiting evidence of practical behavior of virtual episodes and adaptive rates).

strengths: Significant and novel contribution: the paper delivers the first second-order (Q∞) and path-length (V1) regret bounds for online episodic tabular MDPs, and the first variance-aware gap-dependent bound that is polylogarithmic in T within a best-of-both-worlds framework, clearly answering a well-motivated open question posed in the introduction.

Two complementary algorithmic instantiations (global optimization over occupancy measures and per-state policy optimization), both built on OFTRL with log-barrier regularization and adaptive learning rates; the policy-optimization variant includes a genuinely new optimistic Q-function estimator (10) with a clean bias control (Lemma E.2), improving the lower-order term over Dann et al. (2023b).

The theoretical treatment is careful and essentially complete: the OFTRL regret analysis (Appendix C), the OFTRL adaptation of the loss-shifting technique (Lemmas D.1–D.2, requiring a nontrivial modification of Jin et al. (2021) because OFTRL stability depends on shifted losses), and variance-aware bounds in terms of new occupancy-weighted variance measures (Lemma D.5) are all derived rigorously, with detailed supporting lemmas (Appendices D–F).

The upper bounds are complemented by data-dependent lower bounds (Theorems 6.1, 6.2) via a simple but effective truncation reduction, establishing near-optimality of the global-optimization bounds in terms of L*, Q∞, and V1; the gap analysis for path-length bounds is honest and correctly tied to the known √A gap in the bandit literature.

Clear presentation: comparison tables (Tables 1–3) situate the contribution precisely against Zimin & Neu, Lee et al., Jin et al., Luo et al., and Dann et al.; the discussion of variance measures (Section 3, B.2) correctly explains the H²-sharpness relative to Var*_max-based measures.

Limitations are stated transparently: the known-transition assumption is explicitly flagged, the H-factor gap for policy optimization and the path-length gap are acknowledged, and extension to unknown transitions is described as open rather than overclaimed.
weaknesses: The setting is restricted to known transitions in layered MDPs; the data-dependent guarantees do not extend to the more practically relevant unknown-transition case, and the paper correctly notes that even first-order best-of-both-worlds guarantees are open there. This limits the immediate applicability of the results, though it is an honest and standard restriction for this line of work.

The policy-optimization results incur an additional factor of H in the leading term relative to global optimization (Theorems 5.2/5.3), and Theorem 5.3's gap-dependent bound carries sizable additional terms (e.g., √(HS²A²C) log^{3/2}(T) and S²A(H²+√A)log²(T)) that can dominate in low-corruption regimes; the variance-aware gap-dependent guarantee for policy optimization is therefore less clean than its global-optimization counterpart.

The gap-dependent bounds still involve additional corruption-dependent terms and, for Theorem 4.2, the variance-aware gap-dependent bound UVar contains an extra √(H·S²A²C) term; the claimed improvement over Jin et al. (2021) is real but the full statement is messier than the leading-term comparison in the tables suggests.

Global optimization requires solving a convex program over the occupancy-measure polytope each episode, which the paper acknowledges is computationally demanding; no discussion of computational complexity of the proposed procedures or any empirical validation is provided (acceptable for a theory paper, but worth noting for reproducibility of practical claims).

Several minor inconsistencies suggest insufficient polish: Remark D.11 (restatement of Remark 4.3) states the improved UVar still contains HV^c(s) instead of V^c(s) (a factor-H typo), and cross-references occasionally label lemmas as theorems (e.g., 'Theorem E.1' vs Lemma E.1, 'Theorem D.4' vs Lemma D.4); none affect the results but should be fixed.

The lower bounds are derived for particular hard instances via truncation; they show matching dependence on the complexity measures for the constructed instances, but the path-length upper bound leaves an explicit √(SA/H)-factor gap, so optimality is not fully settled for that measure.

strengths: The paper introduces genuinely new complexity measures for online tabular MDPs (second-order quantity Q∞, path-length measure V1, and occupancy-weighted variance measures V and V^c) and delivers the first second-order and path-length regret bounds for online episodic MDPs, closing a gap with the broader online learning literature.

The main theorems unify a large set of previously fragmented guarantees: a single OFTRL-based algorithm (with two loss-prediction schemes) simultaneously achieves first-order, second-order, and path-length bounds in the adversarial regime and variance-aware gap-independent and gap-dependent (polylog T) bounds in the stochastic regime with adversarial corruption. This improves over Jin et al. (2021) by avoiding the 1/min Δ dependence and over Dann et al. (2023a) in lower-order terms.

Both a global-optimization and a policy-optimization instantiation are provided. The new optimistic Q-function estimator (14) with a controlled optimism margin is a technically interesting contribution that lets the policy-optimization analysis go through despite the bias introduced by loss predictions in OFTRL.

The paper provides matching (up to logs, and up to a documented sqrt(SA/H) gap for path-length) regret lower bounds, showing that the global-optimization upper bounds are nearly optimal in L*, Q∞, V1, and V. The variance measure comparison in Section B.2 convincingly situates V and V^c as H^2-sharper analogues of existing total-variance measures.

The paper is well written with clear tables comparing against prior art, complete detailed proofs (~70 pages of appendix with all constants tracked), a notation table, and honest discussion of limitations (known transitions, H-gap in policy optimization, path-length gap mirroring bandits).
weaknesses: The restriction to known transitions is a substantial scope limitation: the practically important setting is unknown transitions, and the authors themselves note that even first-order data-dependent guarantees under unknown transitions remain open for policy optimization. The known-transition setting isolates loss-estimation difficulty, but this weakens the applied relevance of the results.
All guarantees are in expectation rather than with high probability, which limits comparability with the high-probability lines of work (e.g., Lee et al. 2020) the paper builds on.

The policy-optimization results pay an extra factor of H relative to the global-optimization bounds and a sqrt(log^2 T) factor; the path-length bound leaves a sqrt(SA/H)-dependent gap. These gaps are honestly documented, but they mean the more computationally practical of the two approaches delivers noticeably weaker adaptive guarantees.

The adversarial lower bounds (Section 6) follow from a fairly simple truncation reduction of the standard minimax instance rather than deeper instance-specific constructions; this is adequate but means the lower-bound contribution is modest in technique, and the stochastic variance lower bound (Theorem 6.2) applies only to V (not V^c), leaving the gap-dependent variance bound without a matching lower bound.

Global optimization requires solving a large convex program over the occupancy polytope each episode, limiting scalability; no computational considerations or experiments are provided (understandable for a theory paper, but relevant to the significance of the policy-optimization variant).

strengths: The paper establishes the first second-order (Q∞) and path-length (V1) data-dependent regret bounds for online episodic tabular MDPs, extending a well-developed line of bandit results (Hazan & Kale; Wei & Luo; Ito et al.) to the MDP setting — a genuine gap in the literature.

It introduces new occupancy-weighted variance measures V and V^c that are H^2-sharper than the standard Var^*(s,a)-based measures, and achieves variance-aware gap-independent bounds (√(SA(VT+C))) and variance-aware gap-dependent bounds with polylog(T) dependence within an FTRL-based analysis, which the authors credibly claim is a first for MDPs.

The contribution is complemented by matching (up to logarithmic factors) lower bounds for L*, Q∞, V1, and V (Theorems 6.1–6.2), so the global-optimization guarantees are nearly optimal; the remaining √(SA/H) path-length gap is honestly attributed to a known bandit-level gap.

Both the global optimization and policy optimization variants are developed, with a technically nontrivial new optimistic Q-function estimator (Eq. 14) that corrects the bias induced by OFTRL loss predictions, plus careful treatments of virtual episodes and dilated bonuses.
The known-transition restriction is stated clearly upfront with a candid discussion (Section 1 and B.1) of why extending to unknown transitions is open, rather than hidden.

The proofs (Sections C–G) are detailed and largely self-contained, with careful lemma chains and consistent constants; the comparison tables (Tables 1–3) make the improvements over Jin et al. (2021), Luo et al. (2021), and Dann et al. (2023a) transparent, including the removal of the 1/min ∆ dependence.
weaknesses: The known-transition assumption substantially limits practical relevance; the unknown-transition case — where transition-estimation errors would interact with the data-dependent measures — remains open, so the applicability of the refined bounds is confined to a stylized setting.

The work is largely an adaptation of existing machinery (OFTRL with log-barrier and gradient-descent predictions from Ito (2021); Tsuchiya et al. (2023); loss-shifting from Jin et al. (2021); dilated bonuses and virtual episodes from Luo et al. (2021); Dann et al. (2023a)) rather than a fundamentally new technique; the novelty lies in careful refinement and combination.

The path-length upper bound carries a √(SA/H) gap relative to the Ω(√(H V1)) lower bound, and policy optimization bounds retain multiplicative H factors and log^2(T) factors, so the guarantees are less sharp than the best-possible picture.

The gap-dependent variance bounds depend on HV^c(s)/∆(s,a) in general, with the H-improvement only under an additional uncorrelatedness assumption across layers (Remarks 4.3/5.4), which narrows when the refined variance measure actually helps.

The paper is purely theoretical with no experiments (acceptable for this genre, but it provides no evidence on the practical behavior of the algorithms, e.g., whether virtual episodes or the min-structured learning rates are well-behaved in practice).

Some of the stochastic-regime gains over Jin et al. (2021) are refinements (removing 1/min ∆ in favor of U or UVar) whose advantage in concrete instance families is not quantified beyond worst-case comparisons.

strengths: Introduces genuinely new complexity measures for online tabular MDPs (second-order quantity Q∞, path-length V1, occupancy-weighted variance V and V^c) and provides the first second-order and path-length regret bounds for online episodic tabular MDPs, addressing a recognized gap relative to the broader online learning literature.

Delivers a single best-of-both-worlds guarantee covering first-order, second-order, path-length, variance-aware gap-independent, and variance-aware gap-dependent (polylog T) regret, replacing previously separate algorithms (e.g., Lee et al. 2020; Dann et al. 2023a; Jin et al. 2021), and improves the gap-dependent bound of Jin et al. (2021) by removing the dependence on 1/min_{s,a} Δ(s,a).

Both global-optimization and policy-optimization variants are provided, with a technically interesting new optimistic Q-function estimator (Algorithm 2, (14)) whose controlled optimism (Lemma E.2) enables the bias analysis, and an OFTRL-compatible adaptation of the loss-shifting technique of Jin et al. (2021).

Complementary information-theoretic lower bounds (Ω(√SA L*), Ω(√SA Q∞), Ω(√H V1), Ω(√SA VT)) establish near-optimality of the global-optimization upper bounds up to logarithmic factors, and the paper honestly identifies the remaining √(SA/H) gap for path-length bounds and the H-gap for policy optimization as consistent with known bandit/MDP gaps.

Extensive and apparently careful supporting material: ~58 pages of appendix with detailed proofs, comparison tables for upper and lower bounds, a notation summary, and a clear discussion (Section B.2) of how the proposed variance measures relate to and improve upon Var*(s,a)-based measures (H²-sharper in the known-transition setting).

The known-transition scope restriction, the open unknown-transition problem, and the technical obstacles (data-dependent control of transition-estimation errors) are transparently and fairly discussed in the introduction and conclusion.
weaknesses: The restriction to known transitions substantially limits practical relevance, since in most applications the transition kernel is unknown; while honestly acknowledged, this means the strongest contribution lives in a setting that partially serves as a stepping stone rather than the end goal.

The adversarial lower bounds rely on a very simple truncation reduction (applying the minimax bound of Lemma G.2 on a prefix and zeroing losses afterward); this makes the lower-bound contribution technically light, and no lower bound is provided for the variance-based gap-dependent measure U_Var (in terms of V^c).

The path-length upper bound retains a √(SA/H) gap against the lower bound, and the policy-optimization bounds carry an extra factor of H plus sizable lower-order terms (e.g., H^{5/2}S^{3/2}A log²(T)), so adaptivity in some regimes is not tight.

The gap-dependent variance bounds depend on the corruption level C and, under the layer-independence assumption of Remarks 4.3/5.4, improve by a factor of H; outside that assumption the bounds are weaker, and the paper does not explore whether the independence assumption can be relaxed.

The full proofs are too long to verify exhaustively in review; some constant-level claims (e.g., those in Lemma E.3 and the virtual-episode analysis) are intricate, and reproducibility rests on the correctness of these lengthy derivations. No empirical evaluation is provided, which is acceptable for a theory paper but leaves the practical significance of, e.g., the virtual-episode mechanism untested.
